title: Fraction to Per Cent
context: Grade 5, the pages on fractions as per cents. An adult sees two methods. What the pages are doing is making hundredths: an equivalent fraction over 100 names the per cent by its numerator, which works when the denominator, in lowest terms, goes into 100. The other method multiplies the fraction by 100 and writes the % sign, and the two are kept apart.

writeup.why: Write a fraction as a per cent through an equivalent fraction over 100 when its denominator goes into 100, simplify first when it does not, and use the bracketed method with the % sign last. A mixed number goes past 100%.
writeup.look: A fraction card over a bar of the same whole, the row of Times buttons, the Makes 100 counter, and on the later phases the brackets of the other method and a second whole bar.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only: 'Fraction to Per Cent' in ink at the far left, a small dot set clear of the name, the phase title beside the dot on the same line, the host's navigation, and sound and restart as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at x 64, y 108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: the denominator the fraction card has reached. It is never a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at x 64, y 202. The fraction card stands at x 110, y 230, 200 by 150, its numerator deep blue over the denominator. The bar lies under it at x 110, y 420, 600 long and 70 tall, labelled Whole and 100%, cut into as many equal parts as the denominator says, with the shaded parts deep blue. The Makes 100 counter stands at x 360, y 250 and goes green when the denominator reaches one hundred. The row of Times buttons runs along y 640 from x 110, each labelled in words. When both terms grow, the words Both terms light vermilion over the card, and the bar is recut into more, smaller parts while its shaded length holds still. The Divide by HCF and Times 100 buttons stand at x 760, y 250 and x 760, y 330. The brackets of the other method are written at x 760, y 440, the times one hundred step vermilion and the % sign in ink after the closing bracket. On the fourth phase a second whole bar joins at x 110, y 520, and the Unmix button stands beside the card. The per cent reached is green. Down the right of the canvas, in the same rectangle on every phase and never animated in or out, the question sits above the answer slot at x 1186, y 250 (356 by 92) that holds what the child has given, and under it the pad at x 1170, y 368 (388 by 363). The pad is ten number keys with a fraction bar key, a space key for a mixed number and a % key. The footer runs 758 to 900: the voice caption at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling, and the phase bar at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Content colours are the chapter's own, and the tools of this chapter share them. The part the question gives, as shaded cells, a fraction, a decimal or an amount, is deep blue, labelled Given. The per cent, fraction or decimal the working reaches, and what is left after a part is used, is green, labelled Answer or Left. Both terms multiplied or divided by one number, and the times one hundred step before the % sign, are vermilion, labelled Both terms or Times 100. A unit fact that puts two amounts in one unit is violet, labelled Unit fact. The part used, taken away or not won is rose, labelled Used or Not won. The step, cell or number being worked on now is amber. A zero holding a place open inside a decimal is grey, labelled Place holder, and nothing else on the stage is ever grey. An unshaded cell of a whole stays warm white inside its near-black outline, the % sign is near-black ink, and anything dimmed fades to half strength rather than turning grey. Chrome never borrows one of them, and each reading survives with the colour taken away, because a part is told by its written label before it is told by its colour.
writeup.finish: The card shows the last fraction beside its equivalent over 100 and its per cent, with the bracketed line of the other method under it.

source_tool.description: A fraction card stands at the top left of the working area, the numerator deep blue over the denominator. Under it lies a bar 600 long, labelled Whole and 100%. The bar is cut into as many equal parts as the denominator says, with as many shaded deep blue as the numerator says. A row of Times buttons, times two, four, five, ten, twenty, twenty-five and fifty, multiplies both terms by that number: the words Both terms light vermilion, the card rewrites itself, and the bar is recut into more, smaller parts while the shaded length stays still. A Makes 100 counter beside the card asks what times the denominator makes 100, and goes green when the denominator reaches 100. A Divide by HCF button divides both terms by their HCF first. A Times 100 button writes the fraction inside brackets with times 100, works out the product, and writes the % sign after the closing bracket. On the last phase an Unmix button turns a mixed number into an improper fraction and a second whole bar joins the first. A number pad types a fraction, a mixed number or a per cent. The running count at the top left of the canvas is the denominator the card has reached.
source_tool.art_direction: Paper strips folded on a desk / Picture book

style.text: Least text. One header line, short labels, nothing else. The voice carries the teaching and the caption carries the voice.

stage.note: Every coordinate is authored in 1600x900, so a smartboard and a phone in landscape get one composition. Nothing scrolls. The three bands below are the settled layout, taken from Two Hundred Trail in Class 3 chapter 3 once it was finished; a tool that has to depart from one of them says in its own writeup.stage which band it changed and why.

bands.canvas: 92 to 746. One rounded panel holding everything the child works on.
bands.footer: 758 to 900. The voice at the far left, the phase bar at the right.
bands.header: 0 to 80. One line, and only one.

zones.bar: the phase bar at the right of the footer, the question count under it
zones.pad: under the slot, and furniture on every phase: twelve keys three across where a number is asked for, a word pad where a name or a rule is
zones.name: the tool name at the far left of the header, a measured dot set clear of it
zones.runs: the running count, on the canvas at its top left, never up in the chrome. It counts the thing the tool is actually building; where a tool has nothing to count that corner carries the record being kept instead, and that tool's own stage says so
zones.slot: the question and the child's answer, fixed down the right of the canvas
zones.work: the working area, one thousand and eighty-six by five hundred and twenty-eight
zones.title: the phase title beside that dot, on the same single header line
zones.voice: the caption at the far left of the footer, its speaking dot beside it
zones.chrome: again, sound and restart, as round controls at the far right of the header

stage.furniture: The working area is furnished from the first frame. What waits for the child is the count, not the picture: the panels, the slot and the pad are all up and empty before anything is asked.
stage.noSidebar: There is no sidebar. The canvas takes every unit the chrome can spare, because the working area is the tool.
stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box anywhere on the stage. The score leaves on the finished event and it is the host that decides whether to show it, so a child working is never watching a number that judges them.

style.motion: Animate only what carries meaning. Anything that is not changing does not move. Every reward is the maths itself moving, never confetti. Honour prefers-reduced-motion.
drawing: Hand-built inline SVG. No assets and no network, so a school cart works offline.
Chunky rounded forms and large touch targets. A finger is the pointer, not a mouse.

Drawn things, not abstract boxes: hundred grids of ten rows and ten columns, strips cut into equal cells, fraction bars with their denominator of one hundred built beside them, measuring jugs, tapes and scales with their units written on them.

Every whole is drawn the same size as every other whole it is compared with, and its parts are exactly equal: a strip of ten has ten cells of one width, and a hundred grid is always a full ten by ten.
A whole is always labelled 100%, so the child sees what one hundred per cent means before any part is named.
Where shaded cells are counted, exactly the stated number is shaded, and they stay countable at a glance: full columns of ten first, then single cells.
A product that becomes a per cent is always written with its brackets, and the % sign comes last. A decimal reaches a per cent through its hundredths, never by moving anything.
Nothing is animated except the one thing being explained: cells filling a grid, both terms of a fraction growing together, a unit fact rewriting an amount, or a used part lifting away.
style.palette_rule: A chrome colour never fills a cell or a number the child is reading, and a content colour is never used for chrome. This chapter colours the roles a per cent plays in a piece of working: the part the question gives, as shaded cells, a fraction, a decimal or an amount, is deep blue, and the per cent, fraction or decimal the working reaches, with what is left after a part is used, is green; those two are the same two in every tool and every picture of this chapter. Both terms multiplied or divided by one number, and the times one hundred step before the % sign, are vermilion. A unit fact that puts two amounts in one unit is violet. The part used, taken away or not won is rose. The step, cell or number being worked on now is amber. A zero holding a place open inside a decimal is grey. An unshaded cell of a whole stays warm white inside its outline, and the % sign itself is near-black ink. Each role is named in writing first, with the words Given, Answer, Both terms, Unit fact, Used, Not won, Left and Place holder, so the stage still reads with the colour taken away.

rules: Every spoken line is also printed in the caption line at the far left of the footer, so a muted tablet and a child who cannot hear lose nothing.
The caption stays in the footer. Nothing is ever written over the working area.

Numbers are written as words in every line and never as digits, so the voice says four steps and not 4 steps. Handed a digit, a synthesiser reads it in whatever register it likes and the chapter loses the words it is teaching.
The voice never gives the answer. It asks the same question a different way.
It speaks on opening, once when a phase begins, on a miss, and at the finish. It is silent otherwise; a tool that chatters gets muted, and then the first rule is all that is left.
props.muted is honoured at the source, and turning sound off cancels any line already speaking.
voice.where: The caption line sits at the far left of the footer with a small dot beside it that glows while the voice is talking. An again control repeats the last line.
voice.figure: None. The voice speaks with nothing on the stage.
voice.onMiss: Look at the bottom number. What times it makes a hundred?
voice.onNext: A new fraction. Ask about the bottom number first.
voice.opening: A fraction, and a bar of the same whole.
voice.onFinish: You made hundredths, and wrote the per cent sign last.
voice.onFreePlay: Free play. Grow, simplify and bracket any fraction you like.
voice.figure_rule: A figure appears only where the printed chapter puts one and it has work to do. Everywhere else the voice speaks from the caption line with nothing on the stage: a mascot with no job is one more thing competing with the quantities the child is looking at.
voice.voicePreference: an English voice, female where one is offered

placement.where: After the class has folded paper strips into halves, quarters and fifths and written equivalent fractions by hand. The tool is what recuts a bar into hundredths while the shaded part stays still, which paper can only redraw.

answer_key.rule: Multiply both terms by the same number until the denominator is 100, and the numerator is the per cent. This works when the denominator, in lowest terms, goes into 100. When it does not, simplify first by dividing both terms by the HCF, then check again. It never works for 1/3, because 3 does not go into 100. The other method multiplies the fraction by 100 inside brackets and writes the % sign last. Use one method or the other, not both at once. A mixed number becomes an improper fraction first. More than one whole is more than 100%.
answer_key.wrong: The bar is shown again under the child's fraction and under the right one, at the same length, so the two shaded lengths are seen side by side, and the step where the terms were changed is lit amber. Nothing is cleared and nothing is marked.

hostProps.muted: Sound off. Honour it at the source, not by muting an element later. The captions carry on.
hostProps.phase: number, 1-based, which phase to build. The host chooses the activity; the component builds that phase and nothing else and never moves on by itself.
hostProps.device: tablet / web / smartboard. The stage is a fixed 1600x900 that scales; lay nothing out per device.
hostProps.audience: classroom or solo, and ACCEPTED AND NOT ACTED ON. The teach run and the hint ladder run either way. Kept so the contract is one shape across the book, and named here so nobody reads the shape as a promise.
hostProps.learnQuestions: The four worked items, one per phase, supplied by the host.
hostProps.practiceQuestions: The eight practice items, supplied by the host.

phase_mount.run: A phase is a complete activity in itself and it runs once. The teaching and the doing are not two screens and not two modes: the stage is furnished once, the voice talks over it, and the child starts working on the same stage without anything being rebuilt. Whatever the tool as a whole has to say goes into the FIRST phase's teach run, because there is no opening screen to say it on.
phase_mount.idle: NO AUTO-ADVANCE. After firing, the tool goes idle on the settled phase with the child's work still on it, and stops. Where the host supplies onNext it is drawn and it calls the host back; nothing in the component advances a phase.
phase_mount.prop: phase: number, 1-based, matching writeup.phases[].n. Rounded, clamped, and defaulting to 1 when the host sends nothing, so a bare mount is still a working tool rather than a blank screen. Read once: changing which phase a mount shows is a re-mount.
phase_mount.rule: ONE PHASE, ONE MOUNT. The host says which phase to build by passing `phase`, and the component builds that phase and nothing else. It does not know what came before it and it never moves on by itself.
phase_mount.opening: There is no opening panel and no Start button. The host has already chosen the activity, and a cover screen in front of it is a click between a child and the work. writeup.opening is the first frame of every mount rather than a panel of its own.
phase_mount.completion: The terminal event `finished`, with the phase in its detail, fired exactly once and guarded by a one-shot ref that only a restart re-arms, with the chime and the settle OUTSIDE the guard. props.onComplete is called alongside it: the event is the platform's signal and the callback is the host wrapper's, and firing only one of them leaves a child on a tool that never completes.
phase_mount.notInAMount: No finish card and no free play. Both are the host's now, built out of what the events told it. writeup.finish and writeup.freePlay stay as the record of what they are.

shared_state.note: What getState() returns. These names are a contract: the host reads them to persist and resume a child mid-activity, so renaming one breaks resume. `mode` is gone from this list because there is no mode. `phase` is the phase the host mounted, so a resume restores the work inside a phase and the host restores which phase.

agent_control.reason: Every tool in this chapter is child-operated. There is no agent-driven Concept mode, no postMessage command channel and no narration the tool waits on; the adult, where there is one, talks over the tool rather than through it.

steps: The numerator of a fraction over 100 is the per cent, so 13/50 is 26%.
items.question: Write 13/50 as a per cent.
items.checkpoint: Multiply both terms by the same number, so the amount stays the same.
items.misconception: Adding 50 to both terms to reach a denominator of 100, which gives 63/100, a different amount.

steps: 60 does not go into 100, so simplify first.
The HCF of 33 and 60 is 3, so 33/60 = 11/20.
20 x 5 = 100, so multiply both terms by 5: 11/20 = 55/100.
The numerator is the per cent, so 33/60 is 55%.
items.question: Write 33/60 as a per cent.
items.checkpoint: Simplify first, then check that the denominator goes into 100.
items.misconception: Dividing only the numerator by 3 and writing 11/60, which is a smaller amount.

steps: Multiply the fraction by 100, and keep the % sign for the end: 21/35 x 100 = 2100/35 = 60.
Write the product in brackets, then the % sign after them.
items.question: Write 21/35 as a per cent by multiplying it by 100 and writing the % sign.
items.checkpoint: Use one method or the other, and write the % sign last, after the brackets.
items.misconception: Writing 60 with no % sign, which would mean sixty wholes, not a part of one whole.

steps: Write it as an improper fraction first: 1 9/20 = 29/20.
20 x 5 = 100, so multiply both terms by 5: 29/20 = 145/100.
The numerator is the per cent, so 1 9/20 is 145%.
One whole is 100%, so more than one whole gives more than 100%.
items.question: Write 1 9/20 as a per cent.
items.checkpoint: A mixed number is more than one whole, so its per cent is more than 100%.
items.misconception: Turning only the fraction part into a per cent and giving 45%, which leaves out the whole.

learn.shape: Worked items, shown solved, mandatory before practice unlocks.
learn.selection: Fixed order, walking the phases from the first to the last.
learn.content_criterion: One per phase, so Learn walks the whole topic and stops.

items.question: Write 3/6 as a per cent by multiplying it by 100 and writing the % sign.
Why can 1/3 never be written with a denominator of 100 by multiplying both terms by one whole number?
items.final_answer: Because 3 does not go into 100: 3 x 33 = 99 and 3 x 34 = 102, and no whole number times 3 makes 100

items.question: Write 16/40 as a per cent by multiplying it by 100 and writing the % sign.
Is 1 1/10 more or less than 100%? Write it as a per cent.

teaching_notes: Fold paper strips into halves, quarters, fifths and tenths before the tool opens. Ask what times the denominator makes 100 before anything is multiplied, and multiply both terms by it. When the denominator does not go into 100, simplify first and check again; say plainly that one third never gets there. Keep the two methods apart, and write the brackets whenever the fraction is multiplied by 100, so the % sign comes last. A mixed number becomes an improper fraction first. Use fresh fractions: the exercise's own are the child's to convert.
generation_prompt: Build a fraction to per cent tool on a fixed 1600x900 SVG stage. A bar 600 long is labelled Whole and 100%. A fraction card sits over it, and the bar is cut into as many equal parts as the denominator, with the numerator's parts shaded deep blue. Times buttons multiply both terms by one number, lighting the words Both terms vermilion, and the bar recuts into smaller parts while the shaded length stays still. A Makes 100 counter asks what times the denominator makes 100. A Divide by HCF button simplifies first, and a one third card climbs past 100 without landing on it. The running count at the top left of the canvas is the denominator reached. Pointer events only, no assets, no network.
